evt-fall-western-rome.why: By the 470s the western empire had lost Britain, Spain, North Africa and most of Gaul to Germanic kingdoms, and with them most of its tax revenue. Real power lay with army commanders. When the general Orestes refused land in Italy to his largely Germanic troops, they rallied behind Odoacer.
evt-fall-western-rome.impact: Odoacer ruled Italy as king, nominally under the eastern emperor, and Roman law, the Senate and Latin continued there for generations. The eastern empire lasted until 1453. Historians still debate whether 476 was a collapse or one step in a slow transformation into the medieval kingdoms.

evt-charlemagne-crowned.why: Charlemagne had conquered the Lombards, Saxons and Bavarians and ruled most of western Christendom. Pope Leo III, attacked by rivals in Rome in 799, fled to him for protection. In Constantinople the throne was held by a woman, Irene, which some in the west chose to treat as vacant.
evt-charlemagne-crowned.impact: The title revived the idea of a western empire and was later claimed by German kings, forming the Holy Roman Empire, which lasted until 1806. It also set a precedent that popes crowned emperors, a claim that fuelled centuries of disputes between papal and imperial authority.

evt-great-schism.why: East and west had drifted apart for centuries over language, the pope's claim to authority over the whole church, a clause added to the creed in the west, and practices such as the use of unleavened bread. Norman conquests in Byzantine southern Italy sharpened the quarrel.
evt-great-schism.impact: Few at the time saw the break as final, and contacts continued. The crusader sack of Constantinople in 1204 made the division bitter and lasting. Attempts at reunion in 1274 and 1439 failed, and the mutual excommunications were only lifted in 1965.

evt-domesday-book.why: William faced a threatened invasion from Denmark in 1085 and needed to know what his kingdom could yield in tax and military service. Two decades of handing land to Norman followers had also left ownership tangled. Commissioners toured the shires and questioned local juries under oath.
evt-domesday-book.impact: The survey gave the Crown a written record of who held what and what it was worth, and it was cited in land disputes for centuries. It shows how completely Normans had replaced the English landholding class, and it remains a key source for historians.

evt-council-clermont.why: The Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos had sent envoys asking for western help against the Seljuk Turks, who had taken most of Anatolia. Urban also hoped to mend relations with the eastern church, strengthen papal leadership and direct the violence of Europe's knights outward.
evt-council-clermont.impact: Tens of thousands took the cross, far more than expected. The First Crusade captured Jerusalem in 1099 and founded four crusader states in the Levant. On the way crusaders massacred Jewish communities in the Rhineland, and the movement shaped relations between Christians and Muslims for centuries.

evt-hijra.why: Muhammad's preaching of one God threatened the Meccan elite, whose standing rested partly on pilgrimage to the city's shrine. After his uncle and protector Abu Talib died, his position became precarious. Leaders in Yathrib, worn down by feuding between their clans, invited him to come as an arbiter.
evt-hijra.impact: In Medina Muhammad became a political and military leader as well as a prophet, and the community grew strong enough to take Mecca in 630. The second caliph, Umar, later chose the year of the migration as the starting point of the Islamic calendar.

evt-hannibal-alps.why: Carthage had lost Sicily and its naval supremacy to Rome in the First Punic War, then rebuilt its strength in Spain. When Hannibal took Saguntum, a city under Roman protection, war followed. With Rome controlling the sea, an overland march was his way to strike Italy itself.
evt-hannibal-alps.impact: Hannibal lost many men and most of his elephants in the crossing, yet won crushing victories at the Trebia, Lake Trasimene and Cannae. He stayed in Italy for about fifteen years but could not break Rome's alliances. Rome's final victory at Zama left it dominant in the western Mediterranean.

evt-baghdad-founded.why: The Abbasids had overthrown the Umayyads in 750, drawing much of their support from Iraq and Persia instead of Syria. Al-Mansur wanted a capital away from Damascus, on fertile land where the Tigris and Euphrates run close together and river and caravan routes met.
evt-baghdad-founded.impact: The move shifted the centre of the Islamic world eastwards and brought strong Persian influence into its government and culture. Scholars there translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic, preserving and extending them. The Mongols sacked the city in 1258, ending the Abbasid caliphate there.

evt-genghis-proclaimed.why: Temüjin grew up in poverty after his father's death left the family abandoned by its clan. Over two decades he built a following through alliances and war, defeating the Tatars, Keraits and Naimans in turn. He promoted men for loyalty and ability, which weakened the old tribal ties.
evt-genghis-proclaimed.impact: He reorganised the tribes into army units of tens, hundreds and thousands, issued a common body of law and adopted a script for the Mongol language. His armies then attacked northern China and Central Asia. The conquests killed vast numbers, though estimates vary widely, and also linked trade across Eurasia.

evt-sack-constantinople-1204.why: The crusaders had contracted Venice for a fleet far larger than they could pay for. To settle the debt they first attacked Zara, then agreed to restore a deposed Byzantine prince, Alexios Angelos, in return for money and troops. When he could not pay and was overthrown, they attacked.
evt-sack-constantinople-1204.impact: The victors divided Byzantine lands, setting up a Latin Empire and giving Venice valuable ports and islands. Treasures such as the four bronze horses went to Venice. The Greeks retook the city in 1261, but the weakened empire fell to the Ottomans in 1453.

bat-salamis.why: Xerxes invaded to punish Athens for backing the Ionian revolt and to avenge the Persian defeat at Marathon ten years earlier. Athens had recently spent a rich silver strike from its mines on a large fleet of triremes. With Athens evacuated and burned, the Greeks staked everything on the sea.
bat-salamis.impact: Xerxes returned to Asia with part of his force, and the army he left behind was beaten at Plataea the next year. Athens, whose ships had formed the largest contingent, emerged as a naval power and soon led the Delian League, the basis of its later empire.

bat-red-cliffs.why: The Han dynasty was collapsing into rule by rival warlords. Cao Cao, who controlled the emperor and had unified the north, moved south and took Jing province. Sun Quan and Liu Bei, each too weak alone, allied against him. His northern troops were tired, sick and unused to river warfare.
bat-red-cliffs.impact: Cao Cao withdrew north and never again came so close to unifying China. Liu Bei went on to take territory in the west, and by the 220s three rival states, Wei, Shu and Wu, divided the country. Details are uncertain, as much of the popular story comes from a later novel.

bat-manzikert.why: Turkish raiders had been pushing into Byzantine Armenia and Anatolia for years, while the empire's army had been neglected and its court was divided. Romanos IV marched east to secure the frontier fortresses. A large detachment failed to rejoin him, and a rival commander withdrew the reserve during the battle.
bat-manzikert.impact: Alp Arslan released the emperor on fairly mild terms, but Romanos was deposed and blinded on his return. The civil wars that followed did more damage than the battle, leaving Anatolia poorly defended. Within a decade Turkish groups held most of it, founding the Sultanate of Rum.

bat-hattin.why: Saladin had united Egypt and Syria, surrounding the crusader states. A truce broke down after Reynald of Châtillon attacked a Muslim caravan. Saladin then besieged Tiberias to draw the crusaders out, and King Guy, after heated debate, marched his army across dry country in midsummer to relieve it.
bat-hattin.impact: With their garrisons emptied to fill the army, most crusader towns and castles surrendered quickly. Saladin spared many captives but had the Templar and Hospitaller knights executed. The Third Crusade recovered a coastal strip, with Acre as its capital, but not Jerusalem.

bat-ain-jalut.why: Hülegü's Mongols had destroyed Baghdad in 1258 and taken Aleppo and Damascus. When the Great Khan Möngke died, Hülegü withdrew most of his army eastwards, leaving a smaller force under Kitbuqa. Sultan Qutuz executed the Mongol envoys who demanded his surrender and marched into Palestine.
bat-ain-jalut.impact: The Mamluks took Syria, and within weeks their general Baybars murdered Qutuz and made himself sultan. The Mamluks went on to repel further Mongol attacks and to take the last crusader strongholds by 1291. Their sultanate ruled Egypt and Syria until the Ottoman conquest of 1517.

bat-grunwald.why: The Teutonic Order had built a state on the Baltic by fighting pagan Prussians and Lithuanians. Lithuania's conversion to Christianity and its dynastic union with Poland in the 1380s removed the Order's justification for war. Fighting broke out over Samogitia, a region both sides claimed.
bat-grunwald.impact: The Order kept most of its land in the peace of 1411 but owed heavy payments that strained its finances and its subjects' loyalty. After a later war it ceded western Prussia to Poland in 1466. The Polish-Lithuanian union became a leading power in eastern Europe.

ppl-cicero.why: Cicero's family belonged to the equestrian order in a provincial town and had no senators among its ancestors. As a so-called new man he could not rely on birth or military glory, so he built his career on advocacy, studying rhetoric and philosophy in Rome and Greece.
ppl-cicero.impact: As consul in 63 BCE he suppressed Catiline's conspiracy. After Caesar's murder he attacked Mark Antony in a series of speeches and was killed on Antony's orders in 43 BCE. His works brought Greek philosophy into Latin, and their rediscovery by Petrarch helped inspire Renaissance humanism.

ppl-marcus-aurelius.why: He was born into a wealthy senatorial family of Spanish origin with ties to the emperor Hadrian. Hadrian noticed the serious boy and, when arranging the succession in 138, had his heir Antoninus Pius adopt Marcus. He was then prepared for rule for over twenty years.
ppl-marcus-aurelius.impact: He reigned from 161 to 180, at first jointly with Lucius Verus, and spent years campaigning on the Danube. Unlike his predecessors he was succeeded by his own son, Commodus, whose troubled rule is often taken to mark the end of Rome's most stable era.

ppl-augustine.why: His father was a pagan of modest means and his mother, Monica, a devout Christian. The family stretched itself to give him a rhetorical education at Carthage. He taught in Rome and Milan, followed Manichaeism for some years, and was baptised by Bishop Ambrose in 387.
ppl-augustine.impact: His teachings on original sin, grace and free will became central to western Christianity and were later drawn on by both Catholic and Protestant thinkers, including Luther and Calvin. His arguments about when war can be justified fed into the later just war tradition.

ppl-hadrian.why: His family came from Italica in Roman Spain, and ancient sources disagree on whether he was born there or in Rome. Orphaned at about ten, he became the ward of his father's cousin Trajan, the future emperor, and rose through army and government posts under him.
ppl-hadrian.impact: On succeeding Trajan in 117 he gave up the newly conquered lands in Mesopotamia. He rebuilt the Pantheon in Rome and built a great villa at Tivoli. His plans for Jerusalem helped provoke the Bar Kokhba revolt, which Rome crushed with heavy loss of life.

ppl-petrarch.why: His father, a Florentine notary, had been exiled from Florence in the same political purge as Dante, so Petrarch was born in Arezzo. The family later moved near Avignon, then the seat of the popes. He was sent to study law but preferred Latin literature.
ppl-petrarch.impact: His Italian poems to Laura were imitated across Europe and shaped the sonnet later taken up by English poets. In 1345 he found a collection of Cicero's letters at Verona. His friend Boccaccio and later scholars carried on his search for, and study of, ancient texts.

tec-printing-press.why: Gutenberg, trained in metalworking, combined a hand mould for casting identical metal letters, an oil-based ink and a screw press of the kind used for wine. Paper was by then widely made in Europe, and growing towns and universities wanted more books than scribes could copy.
tec-printing-press.impact: Around 180 copies are thought to have been printed, on paper and vellum, and about a quarter survive in whole or part. Gutenberg lost much of his workshop to his financier Johann Fust after a lawsuit. Cheaper books spread literacy and later carried the ideas of the Reformation.

tec-gunpowder-formula.why: Chinese alchemists searching for elixirs had found by the ninth century that mixtures of saltpetre, sulphur and carbon burned fiercely. The Song dynasty, under pressure from the Liao and Western Xia states on its northern borders, ordered a compendium of military knowledge that included the new fire weapons.
tec-gunpowder-formula.impact: The early recipes made incendiaries and weak explosives, not a propellant for guns. Over the following centuries Chinese armies developed fire lances, bombs and then true firearms. Knowledge of gunpowder reached the Islamic world and Europe in the thirteenth century.

tec-su-song-clock.why: Chinese emperors depended on accurate calendars and astronomical observation, which were tied to their claim to rule with heaven's approval. The Song court commissioned Su Song, a senior official, to build a new instrument. He drew on earlier Chinese water clocks and armillary spheres and worked with skilled engineers.
tec-su-song-clock.impact: Su Song described the clock in an illustrated treatise, which is why its workings are known today. The tower was dismantled after the Jurchen Jin captured Kaifeng in 1127 and was never successfully rebuilt. The treatise also shows an early chain drive. Any influence on European clocks is unproven.

art-hagia-sophia.why: The previous church on the site was burned down in the Nika riots of 532, which nearly cost Justinian his throne. He ordered a far grander replacement at once and chose two men trained in mathematics, Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, as its designers.
art-hagia-sophia.impact: The first dome collapsed in 558 after earthquakes and was rebuilt higher. The building was the seat of the Orthodox patriarch and the setting for imperial coronations. After 1453 it became a mosque and a model for Ottoman architects, then a museum in 1935 and a mosque again in 2020.

art-notre-dame.why: Paris was growing fast as the seat of the French kings and a centre of learning, and its old cathedral looked small beside it. The new Gothic style, first seen at nearby Saint-Denis in the 1140s, used pointed arches and rib vaults to build taller, lighter churches.
art-notre-dame.impact: Its builders were among the first to use flying buttresses on a large scale. Damaged in the French Revolution, it was saved from neglect partly by Victor Hugo's 1831 novel and restored by Viollet-le-Duc. After the fire of 2019 destroyed the roof and spire, it reopened in 2024.

phi-city-of-god.why: Refugees from Italy reached North Africa carrying the charge that Rome had been safe while it honoured its old gods. An imperial official, Marcellinus, asked Augustine to reply. He wrote the work in instalments alongside his duties as bishop, and it grew to twenty-two books.
phi-city-of-god.impact: By separating the fate of the church from that of any state, the book helped Christianity make sense of the western empire's decline. Medieval popes and kings both cited it in arguments over authority. Augustine died in 430 while the Vandals were besieging Hippo.

con-tenochtitlan.why: Cortés reached Mexico in 1519 against his governor's orders and found many peoples resentful of Aztec tribute demands. The Tlaxcalans became his main allies and supplied most of the besieging force. A smallpox epidemic in 1520 killed many of the city's defenders, including the ruler Cuitláhuac.
con-tenochtitlan.impact: The last ruler, Cuauhtémoc, was captured and later executed. The territory became New Spain, governed from Mexico City for three centuries. Epidemics, forced labour and war caused a steep fall in the Indigenous population, though estimates of its scale vary, and Catholicism and the Spanish language spread widely.

con-panama-canal.why: A French company under Ferdinand de Lesseps tried to dig a sea-level canal in the 1880s and went bankrupt amid disease and landslides. The United States took over in 1904 after backing Panama's separation from Colombia. Controlling the mosquitoes that carry yellow fever and malaria made the work possible.
con-panama-canal.impact: The United States governed a Canal Zone across Panama, a lasting source of resentment there. Under treaties signed in 1977 the canal passed to Panama at the end of 1999. It remains a major route for world shipping and was widened with larger locks in 2016.

con-brazil-independence.why: The Portuguese court had fled Napoleon to Rio de Janeiro in 1808, and Brazil was raised to a kingdom alongside Portugal in 1815. After the king returned to Lisbon in 1821, the Portuguese parliament tried to reduce Brazil's status again and ordered Pedro home. He refused.
con-brazil-independence.impact: Independence came with far less fighting than in Spanish America, and Brazil stayed one large country instead of splitting into several republics. Portugal recognised it in 1825. The monarchy kept slavery in place until 1888 and was itself overthrown the following year.

con-machu-picchu.why: Bingham was in Peru looking for Vilcabamba, the last refuge of the Incas after the Spanish conquest. The site had been built in the fifteenth century, probably as an estate for the emperor Pachacuti, and was abandoned around the time of the conquest. Local people knew it and farmed its terraces.
con-machu-picchu.impact: Bingham returned with support from Yale and the National Geographic Society to clear and excavate the site, and took thousands of objects to Yale. After a long dispute these were returned to Peru from 2011. The site became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983 and Peru's best-known attraction.

con-suez-canal.why: The French diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps won a concession from Egypt's ruler Said Pasha in 1854. His company was financed largely by French investors and the Egyptian government, and much of the early digging was done by Egyptian forced labour. Britain at first opposed the project.
con-suez-canal.impact: Egypt's debts forced its ruler to sell his shares to Britain in 1875, and British troops occupied the country in 1882. The canal became Britain's main route to India. Egypt nationalised it in 1956, setting off the Suez Crisis, and it still carries a large share of world trade.

con-mansa-musa.why: Mali controlled the routes that carried gold from West African goldfields to North Africa, along with salt and copper. Its rulers had been Muslim for generations, and the pilgrimage to Mecca is a religious duty. The journey also displayed Mali's standing to other Muslim powers.
con-mansa-musa.impact: Musa brought back scholars and an Andalusian architect, and is credited with building the Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu, which grew as a centre of learning. A Catalan map of 1375 shows him holding a gold nugget. European interest in reaching African gold directly grew in the following century.

con-ghana-independence.why: Gold Coast soldiers returned from the Second World War to few jobs and rising prices, and riots in Accra in 1948 pushed Britain towards reform. Nkrumah founded the Convention People's Party in 1949 and led strikes and boycotts. His party won elections in 1951, 1954 and 1956.
con-ghana-independence.impact: The new state took its name from a medieval West African empire. Most British and French colonies in Africa followed within a few years, with seventeen countries becoming independent in 1960. Nkrumah promoted African unity but grew authoritarian and was overthrown in a coup in 1966.

con-meiji-restoration.why: American warships under Commodore Perry pressed Japan to open ports in 1853 and 1854, and the trade treaties that followed were widely seen as humiliating. The shogunate's failure to resist discredited it. Samurai from the domains of Satsuma and Choshu allied to overthrow it in the emperor's name.
con-meiji-restoration.impact: The new government moved the capital to Tokyo, abolished the feudal domains and samurai privileges, and introduced conscription, national schooling and, in 1889, a constitution. Japan defeated China in 1895 and Russia in 1905, and began building an empire of its own in Taiwan and Korea.

con-india-independence.why: Decades of campaigning by the Indian National Congress, including Gandhi's mass non-violent protests, had made British rule hard to sustain. The Second World War left Britain deeply in debt. The Muslim League under Jinnah demanded a separate state, and the last viceroy, Mountbatten, brought the handover forward.
con-india-independence.impact: The new border, drawn in a few weeks, split Punjab and Bengal. Estimates vary, but over ten million people moved and several hundred thousand or more died. India and Pakistan fought over Kashmir within months, and India's independence hastened the end of other European empires.

con-australia-federation.why: The colonies charged customs duties on each other's goods and had separate defence forces and immigration laws. Supporters of union argued for free trade between them, shared defence and a common policy restricting non-white immigration. A constitution was drafted at conventions in the 1890s and approved by referendums.
con-australia-federation.impact: The British Parliament passed the constitution into law, and Australia remained within the Empire with the monarch as head of state. Melbourne served as the temporary capital until Canberra was ready in 1927. Aboriginal people were largely excluded from the new nation's political life for decades.

con-treaty-waitangi.why: Growing numbers of British settlers, traders and whalers were arriving, land sales were unregulated and disorder was common. Britain also worried about French interest and private colonisation schemes. London sent William Hobson to obtain sovereignty by agreement with Māori chiefs.
con-treaty-waitangi.impact: The English text ceded sovereignty, while the Māori text granted a lesser right of governance and promised chiefs continued authority over their lands. Large land losses and wars followed in the 1840s and 1860s. Since 1975 the Waitangi Tribunal has heard claims of breaches, leading to settlements.

con-antarctica-sighted.why: Geographers had long supposed that a great southern land existed. James Cook crossed the Antarctic Circle in the 1770s without seeing it but reported abundant seals, which drew sealers south. Tsar Alexander I sent Bellingshausen to explore the far southern ocean for Russia.
con-antarctica-sighted.impact: Who saw the continent first is still debated, since the British officer Edward Bransfield sighted the Antarctic Peninsula days later. Bellingshausen went on to sail right round the continent. Sealers and scientific expeditions followed, and the first undisputed landings on the mainland came later in the century.

con-amundsen-pole.why: Amundsen had planned to go to the North Pole, but switched south in secret after two Americans claimed to have reached it. He was an expert skier who had learned polar travel from Inuit in the Arctic. He relied on sledge dogs and started from the Bay of Whales, closer to the pole.
con-amundsen-pole.impact: His five men returned safely, having killed some of their dogs for food as planned. News of Scott's death the following year overshadowed the achievement in Britain, and historians have argued over the two men's methods ever since. The research station at the pole is named after both.

con-treaty-of-rome.why: The same six states had pooled coal and steel production in 1952, partly to make war between France and Germany impractical. A plan for a joint army failed in 1954, so leaders turned to economic integration. A committee under the Belgian minister Paul-Henri Spaak drafted the proposals.
con-treaty-of-rome.impact: A second treaty signed the same day created Euratom for nuclear energy. Customs duties between the six were removed by 1968 and a common agricultural policy was set up. Britain, Ireland and Denmark joined in 1973, and the Maastricht Treaty created the European Union in 1993.

exp-marco-polo.why: Mongol rule across Asia had made the overland routes unusually safe for merchants. Marco's father Niccolò and uncle Maffeo had already reached Kublai Khan's court on an earlier trading journey. The khan had asked them to return with learned Christians and holy oil from Jerusalem.
exp-marco-polo.impact: Marco dictated his account to a writer named Rustichello while a prisoner of war in Genoa, and it circulated widely in manuscript. Some readers doubted it, and a few scholars still question parts. Columbus owned an annotated copy, and mapmakers drew on its place names.

exp-ibn-battuta.why: He came from a family of Islamic legal scholars and set out to perform the hajj, the pilgrimage every able Muslim should make once. Training in law was valued across the Muslim world, so he could find work, patrons and hospitality from West Africa to India.
exp-ibn-battuta.impact: He served for several years as a judge in Delhi and later in the Maldives. Back in Morocco, the sultan had his story written down by the scholar Ibn Juzayy. The book, known as the Rihla, is a major source on fourteenth-century Mali, India and East Africa, though some passages may be borrowed.

exp-zheng-he.why: The Yongle Emperor had seized the throne from his nephew in a civil war and wanted to display Ming power and draw foreign rulers into paying tribute. Zheng He, a Muslim eunuch from Yunnan who had served him in that war, was a trusted commander.
exp-zheng-he.impact: The fleets brought back envoys, goods and animals, including giraffes from Africa. After the last voyage in the 1430s the court ended them, judging them costly while the northern frontier needed defending. Many records were lost, and the true size of the ships is still debated by historians.

exp-vasco-da-gama.why: Portugal had spent decades pushing down the African coast, and Bartolomeu Dias rounded its southern tip in 1488. The crown wanted direct access to pepper and other spices, which reached Europe through Muslim and Venetian middlemen. A local pilot guided da Gama across from East Africa.
exp-vasco-da-gama.impact: The modest gifts da Gama offered failed to impress Calicut's ruler, and later Portuguese fleets used force. Portugal seized Goa in 1510 and Malacca in 1511 and tried to control Indian Ocean shipping. The Dutch and English followed a century later with their own trading companies.

exp-magellan.why: A treaty of 1494 had divided new discoveries between Spain and Portugal, leaving the eastward route to Portugal. Magellan, a Portuguese navigator out of favour at home, persuaded the Spanish king that the Spice Islands could be reached by sailing west and finding a passage past South America.
exp-magellan.impact: The surviving ship's cargo of cloves was valuable enough to cover the expedition's cost. The voyage revealed the huge width of the Pacific and the strait now named after Magellan. The crew found their calendar a day behind on return. Spain later colonised the Philippines.

exp-drake.why: England and Spain were drifting towards war, and Drake bore a grudge after a Spanish attack on English ships in Mexico in 1568. Backed by private investors and, quietly, by the queen, he sailed in 1577 to raid Spain's poorly defended Pacific ports and shipping.
exp-drake.impact: The treasure repaid investors many times over and helped the queen clear debts. Drake had also claimed a stretch of the Californian coast as Nova Albion. Relations with Spain worsened until open war in 1585 and the Armada of 1588, against which Drake served as vice admiral.

exp-cook-botany-bay.why: The Royal Society and the Admiralty sent Cook to Tahiti to observe the transit of Venus in 1769. Sealed orders then told him to search for a supposed southern continent. After charting New Zealand he sailed west and met the Australian coast, whose western side the Dutch already knew.
exp-cook-botany-bay.impact: Cook claimed the east coast for Britain as New South Wales. After losing its American colonies Britain needed somewhere new to send convicts, and the First Fleet arrived in 1788. For Aboriginal peoples, who had lived there for tens of thousands of years, colonisation brought disease, dispossession and violence.

exp-lewis-clark.why: Jefferson had long wanted the West explored and asked Congress for funds before the purchase was even agreed. He hoped to find a water route to the Pacific for trade, to establish relations with Native nations, and to strengthen American claims against Britain and Spain.
exp-lewis-clark.impact: No easy water route existed, but the journals recorded many plants, animals and peoples new to American science. The party depended on help from Native nations and from Sacagawea, a Shoshone woman. Fur traders and settlers followed, and the journey supported later United States claims to Oregon.

exp-livingstone-stanley.why: Livingstone, a Scottish missionary and campaigner against the East African slave trade, was a celebrity in Britain. With little news from him for years, the owner of the New York Herald, James Gordon Bennett Jr, sent Stanley to find him, expecting a story that would sell newspapers.
exp-livingstone-stanley.impact: Livingstone refused to leave and died in what is now Zambia in 1873. Stanley's fame launched his own expeditions, including work for King Leopold II of Belgium in the Congo. Publicity around both men drew European attention to central Africa. Stanley's famous greeting cannot be verified.

exp-shackleton.why: With the pole already reached, Shackleton aimed to make the first crossing of the continent on foot. The Endurance sailed in 1914 as the First World War began and became trapped in the Weddell Sea ice in early 1915. The crew camped on drifting floes, then took boats to Elephant Island.
exp-shackleton.impact: It took four attempts to get through the ice to the stranded men, finally with a Chilean tug, the Yelcho. Three men of the expedition's separate supply party, on the far side of the continent, did die. The wreck of the Endurance was found in 2022.

exp-lindbergh.why: A New York hotel owner, Raymond Orteig, had offered 25,000 dollars for the first non-stop flight between New York and Paris. Several better-funded crews had crashed or vanished trying. Lindbergh, an airmail pilot backed by St Louis businessmen, chose a single-engine plane and flew alone to save weight.
exp-lindbergh.impact: Interest in flying and investment in airlines rose sharply in the United States in the following years, and Lindbergh toured the country promoting aviation. His later life was darker, marked by the kidnapping and death of his son in 1932 and his opposition to American entry into the Second World War.

exp-earhart.why: Earhart had crossed the Atlantic in 1928 only as a passenger, which made her famous but left her wanting to earn the reputation as a pilot. She had intended to reach Paris, but mechanical trouble and bad weather forced her down in Ireland.
exp-earhart.impact: She received the Distinguished Flying Cross from the United States Congress, the first woman to do so. She used her fame to argue for women in aviation and in other careers. In 1937 she disappeared over the Pacific while attempting to fly around the world.

exp-everest.why: British expeditions had tried the mountain from Tibet since the 1920s, and Mallory and Irvine vanished near the top in 1924. Nepal opened to foreigners around 1950, giving access to the southern route. A Swiss team with Tenzing came close in 1952. The 1953 team, led by John Hunt, had better oxygen equipment.
exp-everest.impact: Hillary was knighted and Tenzing received the George Medal. Hillary later raised funds for schools and hospitals for the Sherpa people. Mountaineering became a large part of Nepal's economy, and thousands have since reached the summit, bringing concerns about crowding, waste and risks to Sherpa workers.

exp-trieste.why: The Swiss physicist Auguste Piccard, father of Jacques, designed the bathyscaphe, which used a large float filled with petrol for buoyancy and a thick steel sphere for the crew. The United States Navy bought it in 1958, during a Cold War push for deep-ocean research, and fitted a stronger sphere.
exp-trieste.impact: The crew reported seeing a flatfish on the bottom, a sighting scientists have since doubted, but the dive showed that vehicles and people could withstand the greatest ocean pressures. The next person to reach the spot was the film director James Cameron, diving alone in 2012.

exp-gagarin.why: The Soviet Union had launched the first satellite, Sputnik, in 1957 and was racing the United States to put a person in orbit. The chief designer Sergei Korolev adapted a military missile as the launcher. Gagarin, a fighter pilot from a farming family, was chosen from a group of twenty trainees.
exp-gagarin.impact: The flight shocked the United States, and weeks later President Kennedy committed it to landing a man on the Moon by the end of the decade. Gagarin became a worldwide celebrity and never flew in space again. He died in a jet training crash in 1968.
